summary: Introduces MSEval, a benchmark of 10 full-stack web projects derived from university capstone assignments, run under 10 multi-agent collaboration topologies (feature squad, pipeline, PM oversight, QA-first, swarming, etc.) in the authors' LegoGent runtime and graded by their LLM-assisted TAgent grader over up to three feedback rounds. Reports that coordination topology shifts score, time and cost as much as model choice.

claims.claim: For identical tasks and models, topology shifts scores by over 30 points.
claims.evidence: §Key Findings: DeepSeek v4 Pro 89.9 (pipeline) vs 43.0 (open-source review) on the instant-messaging project. This is a single project/model pair, mostly single runs; on the 10-project averages (Table 3) the spread is much narrower (e.g. Pro 69.2-86.6; QA-first/rotation 83.3 vs open-source 73.5).

claims.claim: Structured pipelines converge fastest with the highest quality, whereas heavy managerial oversight degrades performance.
claims.evidence: Body text says QA-first and rotation tie highest (83.3) on the 10-mode average; pipeline is best only on some projects (e.g. e-commerce 96.2). Table 3 PM-oversight R3 averages (75.2 Flash, 78.3 Pro, 85.3 GLM) do not show a consistent degradation. Abstract framing is not cleanly supported.
claims.location: Abstract vs §Key Findings, Table 3, App. modes

claims.claim: TAgent feedback drives refinement: 82.0% of 600 adjacent round transitions improve and 94.7% of runs finish R3 above R1.
claims.evidence: §TAgent Feedback Drives Refinement, stated over 300 full-grid runs. Improvement is judged by the same TAgent that produced the feedback (self-evaluation loop).

claims.claim: TAgent scores agree with human TA scores (Spearman 0.87).
claims.evidence: Single sentence in Limitations; no sample size, protocol or per-project breakdown given.

claims.claim: Failures are dominated by functional shortfall and broken cross-agent prerequisites rather than crashes.
claims.evidence: Table 4: 1,440 failing checks; incomplete logic 32.2%, missing features 23.8%, auth/permission 11.9%, prerequisite cascades 11.0%. Labelling procedure and inter-rater agreement not described.

patterns.note: Role/topology choice strongly matters; some multi-agent modes (open-source review, swarming) waste rounds reconciling overlapping changes. No single-agent baseline, so it cannot say whether multi-agent beats one agent.
Pipeline (staged architect->backend->frontend->QA) strong on some projects; PM-oversight mode results are inconsistent across models.
QA-first mode (requirements turned into acceptance targets before implementation) ties for best 10-project mean (83.3) and is strongest on hardest project; single-run evidence.
Requirement documents compiled into weighted rubric checks used both for grading and as ranked repair agenda.
Deploy-and-probe feedback loop over 3 rounds improves scores in most runs, though measured by the same grader.
TAgent uses LLM inspection for UI-state and code checks; validation is a single unreported-n Spearman 0.87 against TA scores.
Reports USD cost and cache-aware token accounting per round; 90-minute per-round cap; shows score frontier differs from cost frontier.
Identifies broken cross-agent API contracts / prerequisites (23% of failures) as the multi-agent-specific failure; layer-specialist mode synchronises at API contracts.

methodology.sample: 10 web projects from university capstone assignments x 10 modes; 5 models reported (Qwen3.6-Flash omitted after scoring 0 everywhere). Instant-messaging project run across all models; full 10-project grid for DeepSeek v4 Flash, Pro and GLM-5.2 (300 runs). Abstract says '100 runs'.
methodology.baselines: No single-agent baseline and no external multi-agent framework baseline; modes compared only against each other inside LegoGent.
methodology.models: Claude Opus 4.8, GPT-5.5, DeepSeek v4 Flash, DeepSeek v4 Pro, GLM-5.2 (Qwen3.6-Flash dropped).
methodology.variance: Three trials only for instant-messaging token/time; other projects rerun only when 'experts flag a test as abnormal'. No CIs or seed variance for score comparisons.
methodology.ablations: Modes are the manipulated variable; no ablation of TAgent feedback content vs bare retry.
methodology.contamination_controls: None discussed; capstone projects are common web-app archetypes (chat, e-commerce, RBAC).
methodology.languages: Web apps (frontend+backend); implementation languages not controlled or reported per run.

standards.artifacts: Benchmark released at github.com/robinren03/MSEval (project specs, mode definitions, scripts per §Introduction).

biases.detail: Mostly single runs per project x mode x model; the headline 30-point swing is one cell pair.
Authors' runtime (LegoGent) executed and authors' grader (TAgent) both scored results and generated the repair feedback whose effect is claimed.
TAgent uses LLM inspection for UI/code checks; human agreement reported as one Spearman figure with no n or protocol.
Abstract calls MSEval 'a rigorous, reproducible standard' and claims pipelines give highest quality, which the body's averages do not show.
Student capstone web apps; 'real-world' overstated relative to industrial codebases.
Abstract '100 runs' vs body '300 full-grid runs'; abstract's pipeline/PM claims differ from Key Findings.

coi.vendor_products_evaluated: Commercial models (Anthropic, OpenAI, DeepSeek, Z.AI, Alibaba) evaluated as subjects; authors' own LegoGent/TAgent tooling.
coi.detail: Academic authors with no model-vendor stake; mild self-interest in promoting their own benchmark/grader.

verdict_reason: Useful cost-aware framing and failure taxonomy for multi-agent topologies, but headline numbers rest on single runs, an LLM-assisted self-built grader with thin validation, no single-agent baseline, and abstract claims that diverge from the body.
applicability: Directionally relevant to how the team might split agent work across ingestion and delivery repos: the finding that layer-split teams lose accountability for end-to-end scenarios, and that 23% of failures are broken cross-agent prerequisites/contracts, argues for owning a feature vertically (ingestion -> content API -> front-end contract) or pinning explicit API contracts before parallel work. QA-first's relative strength is weak support for spec-driven/acceptance-criteria-first workflows. Does not transfer directly: greenfield student web apps built from scratch in one shared repo, not an existing multi-repo Java backend; no Java, no healthcare constraints, and no comparison against a single agent, so it cannot justify adopting multi-agent topologies at all.
